results.isolated_answer: Yes — Lance Twiggs is held constant across both hypotheses in both calculations, and both calculations presuppose exactly two contributors. The FBI report language was read verbatim into the record twice. Towel (Item 7-1): 'Male DNA was obtained from Item 7, sub 1. Item 7, sub 1 was interpreted as originating from two individuals, one of whom is Twiggs. The DNA results from Item 7, sub 1 … are 1.7 octillion times more likely if Twiggs and T. Robinson are contributors than if Twiggs and an unknown, unrelated person are contributors.' Screwdriver handle swabs (Item 8-1): 'Male DNA was obtained from Item 8, sub 1. Item 8, sub 1 was interpreted as originating from two individuals, one of whom is Twiggs. The DNA results from Item 8, sub 1 are 30 quintillion times more likely if Twiggs and T. Robinson are contributors, than if Twiggs and an unknown, unrelated person are contributors.' So Hp = {Twiggs, Robinson}; Hd = {Twiggs, unknown unrelated person}; N = 2 in both. Twiggs appears on both sides; Robinson is the only term that varies. The statistic therefore measures support for Robinson versus an unknown as the SECOND contributor, conditional on Twiggs; it performs no test of Twiggs's own presence. The FBI examiner confirmed the mechanism in her own words: 'if I'm utilizing someone as a known elimination sample, I will apply their DNA profile both to the HP and HD' (Bakker, 06:39:45–06:40:23), HP being 'the prosecution hypothesis' and HD 'the defense hypothesis'; and on the STRmix input sheet for item 7-1 she confirmed 'Assume there are two contributors', Twiggs' known sample 61 entered under HP with HD left blank because 'the defense hypothesis for this situation … is an unknown unrelated individual' (07:10:01–07:11:14). Item identification: 'item seven is the towel' / 'Item eight is the screwdriver' (McBride–Bakker, 08:07:18–21). The examiner is Amanda Bakker, forensic examiner, DNA Casework Unit, FBI Laboratory, Quantico (05:15:30–45).

Bakker, 08:12:48: 'I did not ignore it. Again, given the type of sample, it was an elimination sample. I compared that individual to the DNA profile that I developed and determined that I could conclude that I could utilize him as an elimination sample.'

The procedural posture matters and is verifiable: Bakker was a DEFENCE witness taken out of order to accommodate her travel (McBride, 04:59:43: 'we're going to call an FBI DNA analyst out of order. WHAT 16.2 IS. Judge Graf, on the record: '16.1 is the text messages, 16.2 is Discord chats, and 16.3 is photograph of notes' (day4 01:18:04), confirmed by prosecutor Ballard. Concretely, 16.2 is a set of PHOTOGRAPHS OF LANCE TWIGGS' PHONE SCREEN showing a Discord server thread — Agent Davis: 'it's a photo of Lance's phone'; 'These are the Discord messages that Lance had talked about'; the photos 'were taken by Agent Larson' at Twiggs' first FBI interview and shown back to him at his second, where he confirmed them (day4 02:51:05–02:51:43).

WHO AUTHENTICATED IT, AND ON WHAT BASIS — two witnesses, and the MODE of the first one matters.
• Lance Twiggs — but not live at the hearing. His authentication sits inside State's Exhibit 16, a VIDEO of a recorded statement played in court (Hunt moved to publish it at day4 02:10:29). The recording opens with the interviewer telling him 'This meeting is to use your statement here instead of your testimony at a preliminary hearing', placing him under oath (administered twice, after a microphone failure), giving the false-statement admonition ('may subject you to criminal punishment as a class A misdemeanor'), and noting 'you've also been given a federal agreement and a state agreement granting you immunity from prosecution for materials that you discuss now.' Within that recording (day4 02:21:18–02:24:03) he is shown 'what's been titled 16.2' and says: 'that was the server, like his friend that I was mentioning'; confirms it is his phone ('I'm assuming you recognize it because the big crack up at the top' — 'Mm-hmm'); 'Yeah, this is Discord'; members are 'his friend group. They played D&D together every week'; asked 'So Tyler Icum, who's that?' answers 'That's Tyler Robinson'; and to 'Is that an accurate recording of that thread?' answers 'To my knowledge, yes.'
• Agent Brian Davis — live and under oath (day4 02:50:48–02:53:27, direct by Ms. Hunt): Agent Larson took the photos; Twiggs confirmed them at the second interview; Twiggs 'is a part of' the thread though 'in this section, he doesn't reply to it'; Twiggs identified Robinson's Discord username as 'the Tyler/Ikum, I-K-U-M'; 'is Exhibit 16.2 a fair and accurate representation of that Discord thread?' — 'Yes, it is'; the first message from Tyler is at '7:57 PM' on 'September 11th'.

HOW THE UNDERLYING MESSAGES WERE OBTAINED — the agent's testimony, verbatim (day4 02:52:39–02:52:51): Hunt: 'As part of your investigation, did law enforcement send a subpoena to Discord?' Davis: 'Yes, they did.' Hunt: 'Were these messages recovered via that subpoena?' Davis: 'They were.' Hunt: 'Did you review that?' Davis: 'Yes, I did.'

ADMISSION (day4 02:54:00–02:54:20). Hunt: 'Judge, the state moves to admit State's Exhibit 16.2 and publish it pursuant to court order.' Novak: 'We've already lodged all of our objections on all three phases.' Court: 'Noting the objections, standing objections by defense. State's Exhibit 16.2 is admitted into evidence and may be published only in the gallery, not for distribution on electronic media.' It appears in the closing exhibit roll-call at day4 06:13:12. At the 09-01 hearing the court again allowed 16.2 and 16.3 to be published 'in the courtroom only' (2026-09-01 transcript 02:30:57).

DID THE COURT RELY ON IT IN ITS FINDINGS — yes, on the content. In the 09-01 oral ruling: 'Just before 8:00 PM on September 11th, 2025, a message was sent from Mr. Robinson's account to his Discord group stating, "Hey guys, I have some bad news for you all. It was me at UVU yesterday. I'm sorry for all of this. I'm surrendering through a sheriff friend in a few moments."' And in the count-one analysis: 'These electronic statements are further corroborated by the alleged in-person confirmation to Twiggs the following morning and subsequent message from defendant's Discord account stating, "It was me at UVU yesterday." … this evidence is sufficient at this stage to support a reasonable belief that defendant is the individual who shot and killed Charlie Kirk.'

results.isolated_answer: The stipulation was read into the record on Day 4 of the preliminary hearing by State's counsel Mr. McBride, at transcript timestamps 04:38:54–04:39:48, immediately after Sgt. Faumuina testified that the rooftop/window area had been processed. Its text: "The language of this has been agreed upon by the parties. The parties stipulate that investigators at the crime scene observed latent fingerprints and a palm print on a glass window near the area where the individual landed when the individual jumped from the rooftop of the Losee Center at UVU. SBI Invest fingerprint examiner, Elisa Farmer, examined images of these latent fingerprints and the palm print and determined that only three of the latent prints, 11B, 11C and 11D, were of comparable or of poor comparable value. She excluded Tyler Robinson as the source of any of these three latent prints. Ms. Farmer reviewed other prints on the window and found that they did not have adequate value for comparison. Subsequent examinations of these three latent or actual latent prints by the FBI were inconclusive." So: as to Robinson, the stipulation records EXCLUSION on all three comparable-value latent prints (11B, 11C, 11D) by the state examiner, from images; and as to a later examination by another laboratory, the SAME stipulation records that the FBI's subsequent examinations of those same three prints were INCONCLUSIVE. Both halves are in one continuous paragraph, no intervening speaker. Corroborated on cross: Mr. Burt put to Faumuina that he had "a report that has to do with the latent print report from your people, SBI?" — Faumuina corrected, "It's not SBI, it's actually the state crime lab, but yes, same department" — and Burt characterised it as "detailing the results of that examination, which the stipulation addressed" (06:10:32–06:10:52). results.isolated_answer:
Two DNA analysts testified, one from each laboratory, and both were called by the DEFENCE.

FBI — Amanda N. Bakker, forensic examiner, DNA Casework Unit, FBI Laboratory, Quantico (day2.txt L5129-5145; called out of order as a defence witness, day2.txt L4412). On MECHANISM, unqualified: asked whether her laboratory has a policy on "formal activity level," she said "We do have a policy, and I cannot give an opinion as far as activity level goes" (L5758), because "just because DNA is on an item doesn't necessarily mean that an individual touched it or utilized that item... we do not opine on what activity may have occurred" (L5766). On the State's examination (McBride) she confirmed: "you cannot testify as to what precise action left the DNA on the object, correct?" — "Correct. I cannot" (day2.txt ~L9175). On TIMING she QUALIFIED twice: "I can't give an exact time, but there are some situations" (L5774-5778), and, drawn out by the State, "there are some indicators that may give some information about how long and the conditions under which DNA was placed on an item, like degradation" — "Yes, degradation or the condition of the item" (day2.txt ~L9185-9190).

ATF — Caitlin (Laura Caitlin) Oliver, DNA Section Chief / forensic biologist, ATF Forensic Science Laboratory (day5.txt L651-700; called by Burt for the defence). On MECHANISM, unqualified: "None of the testing that I performed could speak to activity or what activity led to the deposition of the DNA" (L1107); agreed that major/minor descriptors "should not be interpreted in the context of a decision regarding the nature, or the mechanisms, actions, or timing that led to the deposition of the DNA" (L1255-1259); "None of the testing in any of the three reports can answer the question of how and when DNA got deposited. Is that true?" — "That is true" (L1335-1339); "you can't make any assessment of how or when DNA got deposited. Correct?" — "Correct" (L1375-1379); "you can't tell us anything about when the DNA was deposited on the trigger guard or the trigger, correct?" — "Correct" (L2432-2436). On TIMING she too QUALIFIED: "DNA is quite stable over time. It can be broken down due to environmental insults... but I couldn't give you an exact number," and confirmed degradation was present in some samples, including the trigger/trigger-guard sample (L1385-1400, L2404-2420).

NO CONTRADICTION BY ANY WITNESS. The State called only Officer Chris Bagley (day1 L628), Sgt. David Hull (day1 L6299), Agent Brian Davis (day3 L523) and Sgt. Two passages bear on the Dremel.

(1) day4.txt L1131-1145. Asked about the text "Remember how I was engraving bullets?" and whether Robinson had been engraving bullets before, Twiggs answered: "I don't remember exactly when, but he had said he was planning to go hunting with his family. And he asked me if we had a Dremel, because he said he wanted to engrave messages on bullets. Asked how long before September 10th: "I don't remember, because he'd been talking about the hunting/camping trip for a couple months... (2) day4.txt L1487-1511, at the close of the interview. "The Dremel that you talked about, you said he had asked for that, is that right?" — "Mm-hmm." / "And had he told you it was to inscribe bullets?" — "Yeah." / "And so did you have a Dremel then?" — "Yeah. So: yes, asked directly whether Robinson had told him the Dremel was to inscribe bullets, Twiggs answered affirmatively; and yes, he said he told Robinson where it was rather than handing it to him, the tool being in the household-tools section of the lower-basement-level pantry.

results.isolated_answer: Core proposition: yes, both analysts said it. Amanda Bakker (FBI DNA Casework Unit, Quantico — day2) and Caitlin Oliver (ATF DNA Section Chief — day5), BOTH of them defence witnesses examined on DIRECT by defence counsel Michael Burt, each said they could not say what action deposited DNA or when. Bakker: 'Formal activity level is determining an activity that causes DNA to be left behind on an object... We do have a policy, and I cannot give an opinion as far as activity level goes... just because DNA is on an item doesn't necessarily mean that an individual touched it or utilized that item. So because of that, we do not opine on what activity may have occurred.' Oliver: 'None of the testing that I performed could speak to activity or what activity led to the deposition of the DNA'; Q 'you can't make any assessment of how or when DNA got deposited. Correct?' A 'Correct'; Q 'you can't tell us anything about when the DNA was deposited on the trigger guard or the trigger, correct?' A 'Correct.' BUT the agreement was NOT unqualified, and it was expressly revisited by the State. Bakker qualified the timing limit twice on the defence's own direct — 'I can't give an exact time, but there are some situations... an item that's been buried for 10 years... However, I cannot give exact timing' — and then on the STATE's cross (McBride, 08:00:25–08:02:41) gave a further, elicited qualification: Q 'you cannot testify as to what precise action left the DNA on the object, correct?' A 'Correct. I cannot.' Q 'You can't testify about the exact time that DNA was left on an object, right?' A 'Correct.' Q 'But there are some indicators that may give some information about how long and the conditions under which DNA was placed on an item, like degradation?' A 'Yes, degradation or the condition of the item... something that's been left behind 10 years ago, I don't necessarily expect to recover DNA, but something that may have been left yesterday, I might be able to detect DNA.' Oliver likewise bounded persistence ('DNA is quite stable over time. It can be broken down due to environmental insults... but I couldn't give you an exact number'). Responses: the State presented no contrary evidence ('The state has no rebuttal evidence to present at this hearing') and declined to cross-examine Oliver at all (Judge: 'Anything further for this witness?' McBride: 'No.'). No other witness in the banked transcripts touched activity level or deposition timing. However the point was not adopted either: the court's 2026-09-01 bindover ruling recited that 'Defendant's DNA was identified as a major contributor on multiple key components of the firearm, including the stock, grips, butt plate, the trigger, and trigger guard' and that 'the FBI DNA analysis places defendant's DNA on a screwdriver recovered at the crime scene', and the State argued 'when he put his finger on that trigger and he pulled that trigger'. So: unrebutted by evidence, yes; unqualified by the analysts, no.

The testifying agent was Sgt./Agent David Hull, Utah Department of Public Safety, one of the two case agents (day1 06:31-06:41; day2 00:31-00:46). His identifications ran as follows.

BASIS — PERSON. Hull's identification is downstream of the surrender, not of the video. On the evening of 11 September word came from Washington County that someone wanted to turn himself in; the name "Tyler Robinson" was passed to SIAC (the State Information and Analysis Center), which produced a "workup" — driver's-licence record (including a photograph, address and date of birth) and DMV records. Hull: "Once we knew a vehicle that we were looking for and we had an actual image of the individual, then we were able to use that video footage to try and track that specific individual" (day1 06:34:06). So the person-side basis is the DL photograph plus the tracking method he described on day2 — starting from the rooftop video and working "forward through the timeline and backwards through the timeline" (day2 00:41:57) — with clothing continuity ("the individual in the red T-shirt and the shorts and the shoes", day2 00:45:39) and the gait/limp (day2 01:20 ff., 02:23) as the linking features.

BASIS — VEHICLE. "Information that was provided regards to driver's license and Department of Motor Vehicle records, the vehicle fits the description of a vehicle owned by Mr. Robinson" (day2 00:45:14); asked what stood out, "The shape of the vehicle is very distinct, but predominantly the wheels were very distinctive on this version of the vehicle" (00:45:29). The DMV record gave a silver Dodge Challenger with two registered owners, Robinson and his mother (day1 06:33:27-06:33:39).

PHRASING ON THE RECORD — hedged throughout, and the State framed it that way itself: "the individual believed to be Mr. Robinson" (day2 00:31:48); "That's the vehicle that is believed to belong to Mr. Robinson" (00:45:02); "I believe that's Tyler Robinson" (00:45:58); "a compilation ... that depicts the movements of the individual I believe to be Mr. Robinson" (day1 06:42:10); McBride: "let's be clear, this is someone you believe to be Tyler Robinson?" — Hull: "Correct" (day1 06:37:19).

FACIAL IDENTIFICATION — none was offered as a comparison of the surveillance subject's face. No witness on any of the five hearing days or in the 2026-09-01 argument used the term "facial recognition"; Hull was never asked to say he matched facial features in the footage. The record runs the other way: Officer Novak, shown the roof video, was asked "were you able to identify the individual's face?" and answered "No" (day1 04:13:14), likewise no clothing markings and no height; Hull conceded the roof video "as a standalone" was not distinguishable (day2 01:53:51-53), volunteering only that "there was a meeting to discuss perhaps a pattern on the front of the shirt that was observed when the individual was jumping off of the roof."

(1) MATERIAL. At the preliminary hearing the court made ADMISSIBILITY rulings and expressly withheld any ruling on SCIENTIFIC reliability.

WHAT THE COURT RULED. (1) Pre-hearing, the defence moved to have Utah Const. art. I §12, Utah R. Crim. P. 7B and Utah R. Evid. 1102 declared unconstitutional as to reliable hearsay at a preliminary hearing; the motion was 'extensively briefed and argued' and DENIED at docket 631 (McBride, day2 00:17:51). Burt quoted that ruling verbatim on 09-01 (04:51): 'The presumption of reliability is confined to the presumption that the hearsay evidence is admissible. The presumption does not require the magistrate to find the evidence credible... Admissibility and evidentiary weight remain distinct concepts.' (2) Each DNA exhibit was then admitted over the standing objection under Rule 1102: State's Ex. 30 (ATF DNA report) — 'noting the standing objection by defense, I'm going to overrule that objection pursuant to Utah Rule of Evidence 1102' (day4 05:19:18); State's Ex. 33 (ATF forensic-biology report) — 'Court overrules the standing objections and State's Exhibit ... 33 is admitted' (day4 05:33:05); Ex. 31 (FBI DNA) argued and treated under Rule 1102(b)(4) (day2 06:06:35); defence exhibit Baker 4 p.128 (electropherogram) — 'Under Utah Rule of Evidence 1102B4, it says, "Scientific Laboratory of Forensic Reports and Records," I find that this is admissible' (day2 06:26:14). (3) On 09-01 the court rejected all four constitutional attacks (confrontation, counsel, due process, separation of powers) and held Rule 1102 does not displace the magistrate's function; it assigned the ME report to (b)(5), foundation/authenticity to (b)(3), the Twiggs statement to (b)(8), and required any other hearsay relied on to satisfy (b)(9) 'including its reliability requirement' (08:00:22–08:06:00).

WHAT IT DECLINED TO RULE. Scientific validity/reliability of the DNA methodology was litigated at length — PCAST, the 2024 NIST 'Forensic DNA Interpretation and Human Factors' report, the 20%-minor-contributor limit, STRmix non-reproducibility, number-of-contributors subjectivity, the 3-to-2 contributor change — and the court repeatedly refused to reach it, confining itself to the magistrate role under State v. Ramirez, 2012 UT 59 ¶10, and saying the issue was 'not precluding if this were to proceed, if there were a bind over, if there was a trial, that certainly that could be determined' (day2 06:04:00). It then 'sustain[ed] in part and den[ied] in part,' allowing one more question and cutting the line off (day2 06:07:55). No Rule 702 / Rimmasch / Daubert ruling was made on DNA, latent prints or toolmarks; the 09-01 bindover ruling makes no finding on scientific validity.

OBJECTIONS: yes, on both sides. Defence had a written standing objection (filed 2026-07-03, docket 678) noted by the court as in place 'throughout the rest of the preliminary hearing' (day2 00:20:05), plus item-specific objections. The STATE objected repeatedly that the defence's validity questions were '702 territory,' 'beyond the scope of a preliminary hearing,' 'unhelpful... therefore irrelevant' (day2 06:01:41, 05:50, 05:56; day4 07:27:04, 07:58:05; day5 ~01:12).

Six distinct figures exist; only two are independently produced, and they measure different things.

(A) '~160 yards' (=480 ft). SOURCE: the State's Information/PC narrative filed 2025-09-16, §'The UVU Surveillance Investigation': 'Believing the shot came from a rifle because of its sound, he looked for potential sniper positions. He noted a roof area approximately 160 yards away from Mr. Kirk as a potential shooting position and rushed there to look for evidence.' MEASURED: 'a roof area' (unbounded) to 'Mr. Kirk'. BY WHOM: an unnamed 'UVU Officer' — but as narrated by the prosecutor, not quoted from the officer. METHOD: none stated; a naked-eye estimate from an elevated vantage point, seconds after the shot. STATE OF KNOWLEDGE: he was scanning for threats and only inferred a rifle from the sound; the prone position had NOT been located — the same paragraph has him first climbing the railing, then walking to the position and only then noticing 'impressions in the gravel'. No witness gave this figure at the hearing: '160' and 'yards' return zero hits across all five day transcripts.

(B) '~415 feet' slant / '410 feet' horizontal / '~68 feet' elevation. SOURCE: Sgt. Faumuina, day4 (04:37:11-04:38:28): Q 'Were measurements taken from that sniper position to the tent where Charlie Kirk was seated?' A 'Yes.' ... 'the distance from the perch area directly to the tent where Mr. Kirk was sitting was approximately 415 feet... without taking into account the elevation drop, it was actually 410 feet. So just horizontal straight across. And then the elevation difference between that is approximately 68 feet.' MEASURED: the identified perch to the pop-up tent. BY WHOM/METHOD: NOT ESTABLISHED — the question is passive ('were measurements taken'), Faumuina never says he took them, no instrument, technique, date or operator is given, and no cross-examination touched it. He is an SBI sergeant whose 'primary assignment... was to oversee the crime scenes as well as the physical evidence' (day3 ~47:50; day4 04:34:03). STATE OF KNOWLEDGE: the perch had already been found and processed — 'easy to see at night using oblique lighting. We could see disturbances in the gravel on the rear rooftop' (day4 04:35:59).

(C) Derived/downstream, not independent: State's 2026-08-18 reply — '410 feet from Mr. Kirk, Tr. Day 4 at 91:12-92:10'; defence 2026-08-11 brief — 415 ft slope 'PH4:91', 68 ft 'PH4:92', 410 ft; State on 09-01 — '139 yards or 138.33 yards is 415 feet' and 'The angle is 415 feet. It's not 410 feet'; defence on 09-01 — 'approximately 400 feet away'; the court's 09-01 ruling — 'approximately 415 feet from the canopy and approximately 68 feet above it' (08:16:02).

What the parties did with it. State, opening argument 2026-09-01 at 03:51:41: "The defendant's DNA was found all over that gun. It was on the scope, the grips, the stock, and even the trigger." That is precisely the sentence Oliver said an examiner may not assert. Defence named the move: "he's attempting a source attribution there"; "the State is overreading the DNA evidence in this case"; "What Ms. Oliver and Ms. Baker said was that Mr. Robinson was a possible contributor" (04:53–05:00). On rebuttal the State read the report language correctly and at length (06:17:24–06:21:35) and then re-derived the same sentence as an inference: "Reasonable inference? The defendant's DNA was found all over that rifle, that towel, those cartridges, the screwdriver" (06:22:25).

What the court did with it — two registers, in one document. Factual background (oral 07:56:00; written order p. 6) keeps the analysts' register: "The testing provided support for inclusion of Mr. Robinson's DNA on each item" — but mis-assigns the laboratory: "The FBI performed DNA testing on the screwdriver, towel, rifle, spent casing, and three unfired cartridges found near the scene. State's Ex. 30; State's Ex. 31" — when Ex. 30 is the ATF DNA report on the rifle and cartridges. Identity analysis (oral 08:08:34; written order p. 12) switches to attribution: "Defendant's DNA was identified as the major contributor on multiple key components of the firearm, including the stock, grips, butt plate, the trigger and trigger guard… the FBI DNA analysis (State's Exhibit 31) places Defendant's DNA on a screwdriver recovered at the crime scene, with a likelihood ratio exceeding 30 quintillion." Two things are lost there: the LR's conditioning (both propositions in the 30-quintillion calculation assume Twiggs is a contributor, so the figure never tested Twiggs's presence), and the exhibit anchor — the engraving-cutter identification the order attributes to "the toolmark analysis (State's Ex. 32)" is in State's Ex. 34; Ex. 32, which the library holds and I read directly, says only that the marks are "consistent with being produced by engraving and/or rotary cutting tips commonly found installed in handheld rotary tools such as a Dremel tool" and "contain marks of value for comparison if a suspect tool is located."

Public accounts: mixed, drifting the same way. Fox News, "Tyler Robinson's and Lance Twiggs' DNA both allegedly found on key evidence" — "had his suspected killer Tyler Robinson's DNA on it", "Robinson is likely the majority donor" — no likelihood ratio, no mention of the source-attribution limit. SLTrib, KUER and CNN restate the hedged "DNA consistent with Robinson's" and reproduce the one-trillion form.

Verified in both directions: I looked for the opposite drift — any party, court or outlet stating the forensic proposition MORE weakly than the analyst did — and found none. I also logged the fidelity instances: the State's rebuttal reading, the court's background paragraph, and the SLTrib/KUER/CNN restatements.

results.isolated_answer:
The sworn record on Robinson's work and schooling is ONE passage, and it is inside a recorded statement, not live testimony. On Day 4 the State published State's Exhibit 16 (moved at 02:10:29, played from ~02:10:37, concluded 02:33:59) — the recorded interview of Lance Twiggs, taken at the Utah County Attorney's Office (Agent Davis later fixes it to a second interview, April 20, 2026). Twiggs is put under oath twice on that recording (the oath is re-administered at 02:13:37 after a mic failure), given the false-statement admonition (class A misdemeanour / obstruction), and the recording notes he holds federal and state immunity agreements. The examiner is an investigator (Rev labels him 'Speaker 4'), not trial counsel.

The colloquy, day4.txt 02:15:11–02:16:18, verbatim:
Speaker 4: 'And at that time, let's say September of 2025, what were you doing with your life? Were you working, school?'
Twiggs: 'I was working. I was doing bathtub and shower repair and stuff and new construction.'
Speaker 4: 'Okay. How about Tyler?'
Twiggs: 'I think he was both working. I think he was working for an electrician company then, and he was also in a trade school for being a, I don't know, higher ranking electrician. I'm not sure how the trade system works for that.' … 'But yeah, I think he was both.'
Then on his routine: 'I think he'd leave around 7:00 generally and get back around 3:00 to 4:00, depending on where the job was and how long it was for the day. And then on certain days of the week during school semesters, he would then later in the day, I think around 5:00 or 6:00, go to school.'

Reliability as the speaker himself characterised it: four hedges in two sentences — 'I think' (×3), 'I don't know', and the express disclaimer 'I'm not sure how the trade system works for that.' Note the precise scope of that disclaimer: he disclaims knowledge of how the trade/apprenticeship SYSTEM works, not the bare facts that Robinson worked for an electrician company and attended a trade school — though those two are themselves each prefixed 'I think'.

No employer and no school is named — not here and nowhere else in the corpus. Corpus-wide sweep (artifact_search.find, both U+FFFE readings, all 58 banked primary .txt plus all ten transcript files) on 'trade school', 'electrician', 'apprentic', 'vocational', 'technical college', 'tech college', 'Dixie', 'Utah Tech': the ONLY hits anywhere are the two inside this single Twiggs answer. 'occupat' = 0 in day4. The Public Safety Assessment (2025-09-12), the probable-cause affidavit (2025-09-16) and the sheriff's booking record contain no 'school', 'employ', 'student' or 'occupation' string at all. Inside this library, the only restatement is CR-E02 line 205 ('Robinson worked for an electrician company and attended trade school') — which names neither.

So: the employment and trade-school propositions are recorded at the recording layer only — a hedged, immunised, out-of-court sworn statement played as an exhibit, uncorroborated by any named employer, named school, or any other witness.

results.isolated_answer:
Across the five evidentiary days and the 2026-09-01 ruling, the court decided NOTHING about the scientific reliability of the DNA evidence under Rule 702. Every 702 exchange in the record is a scope/relevance objection resolved on scope, and the only reliability the court ever ruled on is Rule 1102 HEARSAY reliability, which is a different question.

What the record actually shows:
• Day 2 (Bakker, the DNA analyst) is where 702 and DNA meet. McBride objects three times that cross has gone 'into 702 material that's not necessary for the probable cause determination' / 'far into 702 territory'. Burt answers '702 deals with reliability of evidence. That's what the court is here to determine.' McBride answers back: '702 deals with admissibility… directly related to admissibility of the testimony at trial.' The court never picks between those readings. At 06:04:00 Graf grounds himself in State v. Ramirez, 2012 UT 59 ¶10 ('the magistrate's role does not encompass an assessment of whether such inference is more plausible…') and says expressly: 'my fear is as we go down further down this path, which again is not precluding if this were to proceed, if there were a bind over, if there was a trial, that certainly that could be determined.' He then disposes of the objections purely procedurally — 05:50:41 'the objection is overruled. You may proceed with that question'; 05:57:47 'as this is the last question, I'm going to overrule the objection, but as a reminder to all parties that this is a probable cause standard'; 06:07:55 'I'm going to sustain in part and deny in part… this would be the last question.' Those are rulings about how long cross may run, not about STRmix, PCAST, number-of-contributors, stochastic thresholds or foundational validity.
• The reliability ruling that DOES exist in this case is a hearsay ruling, and Burt says so on the record at 06:05:02: 'when we objected to the hearsay aspect of these DNA reports and other reports, you ruled that you are the ultimate determiner of the reliability of the hearsay evidence being admitted.' McBride answers under 'Rule 1102(b)(4)'. That is Utah's preliminary-hearing reliable-hearsay rule, not Rule 702.
• The 2026-09-01 bindover ruling contains ZERO occurrences of '702' (and zero of 'STRmix' or 'probabilistic'), verified under both U+FFFE readings. Its reliability analysis runs entirely through Utah Const. art. I §12 and Utah R. Evid. 1102(a), (b) and (b)(9): 'The presumption of reliability is confined to the presumption that the hearsay evidence is admissible…'; 'hearsay in which the Court relies must independently satisfy subsection (b)(9), including its reliability requirement.'
• The one line that could be mistaken for a 702 finding — 'As a gatekeeper, the court has found it reliable. It's been presented. The exhibits have been found reliable' (day5 01:08:08) — is PROSECUTOR Chad Grunander arguing, not the court ruling. Content proves it: the same speaker continues 'this is all couched in the context of a likely forthcoming standing objection that the state may lodge.' Likewise the 'two roles… gatekeeper role on admissibility' framing at day3 15:31 is Ryan McBride's Rule 104(a) argument, not the judge's holding.
The null is therefore real and it is scoped exactly as the item scopes it: scientific reliability, DNA specifically.

results.isolated_answer: Sworn testimony, chiefly from SBI Agent David Hull. Direct (day1.txt 06:29:36–06:32:25): the priority on Sept 10 was "to identify the individual who'd been seen on the roof," tens-to-hundreds of hours of video were reviewed, and "[e]ventually, on the evening of the 11th, we received word from Washington County that an individual in that area had reached out to law enforcement and was wanting to turn themselves in for the incident at UVU" — and with that came the name Tyler Robinson. Cross (day2.txt): asked whether "as of the moment that Tyler Robinson voluntarily surrendered… you all did not know who the shooter was," Hull answered (01:52:15, L2577): "We had identified a person of interest, but we did not specifically know who the shooter was at that time." Asked whether the roof video "as a standalone" was distinguishable, he answered (01:53:53, L2645–2650): "It was not, no" — while noting they did have a person of interest from the stairwell/parking-garage images "released to the press." Asked whether the surrender was "the first moment you ever knew his name connected with this case," he said (02:11:09, L3389): "Aside from the image that we had, that was the first time that we had a name of an individual who had taken responsibility." He also confirmed "no police went to go arrest him"; he came with his parents and walked in voluntarily. Redirect (02:23:13, L3858): "He had informed, I believe, his immediate family that he had been involved in the shooting and that he wanted to turn himself in." Corroboration: UVU Officer Novak testified he could not identify the roof figure's face, clothing markings, or height from the video (day1.txt 04:13:14–04:13:30); Agent Brian Davis testified the family friend Mike Mitchell "helped facilitate working with Tyler and his parents with the Sheriff's Department for Tyler to turn himself in" (day3.txt 49:34, L1433). After the name arrived, the DL/DMV workup let investigators go back through the UVU footage to track Robinson and the Challenger (day1.txt 06:34:06–06:35:55).
results.label: SUPPORTED

Speakers inferred from Q/A structure and content (e.g. the 01:52:00 question is counsel's leading form, the 01:52:15 answer is the witness's qualified reply), not from Rev labels.
results.divergence: The hypothesis is right in substance but flattens a qualification Hull insisted on twice. He did NOT testify that the footage yielded nothing on identity: investigators had "identified a person of interest" and released his images to the press; what the footage could not do, on his account, was produce a NAME or distinguishable features of the roof figure standing alone. So 'surveillance footage on its own was insufficient to identify him' is accurate as to naming/attribution and inaccurate if read as 'yielded no identity material.' Second, the chain ran family → retired-deputy family friend → Washington County Sheriff → SBI, not parent-to-police directly (Davis, day3 49:34; Hull, day2 01:52:32). Third, at the ANALYST layer this establishes the sworn law-enforcement ACCOUNT of their own state of knowledge — it is not independent verification of what every investigator knew on Sept 11.
results.scope_limits: Covers the state of investigative knowledge as of the evening of Sept 11, 2025, as described under oath in July 2026 by Hull (the co-lead case agent), with Novak and Davis corroborating discrete pieces. results.isolated_answer: ATF DNA Section Chief Caitlin Oliver (a forensic biologist in Sept 2025; called by the defence on Day 5) testified (day5.txt 01:38:16–01:38:55, L1217ff): asked whether she uses "a reporting cap in all three of your reports," she said "Yes. So, for our likelihood ratio statistics, we cap the statistic at one trillion. The actual number could be a lot higher. It could be quintillion, octillion. We chose a trillion because it has meaning to people that can understand what a trillion is… so we cap at one trillion." So every ATF conclusion printed as "at least one trillion times more likely" states the lab's reporting ceiling, not the computed figure; the report's own "at least" discloses the truncation. In this case (State's Ex. 30, the ATF DNA report on the rifle and cartridges) seven statistical calculations were put on the record; six are "at least one trillion" — stock/grips + bolt (1.1/1.4), butt plate (1.2), trigger and trigger guard (1.3), fore-end + a .30-06 cartridge (1.5/5.1), barrel + a .30-06 cartridge (1.6/3.1), and underside of the receiver after disassembly + another cartridge (calc 7). The one exception is Calculation 6, Exhibit 1.9, swabs of the optical accessory (scope): "The DNA profile is 6.28 billion times more likely if it originated from Tyler Robinson as a contributor to the major component and three unrelated, unknown individuals…" (Sgt. Faumuina reading, day4.txt L4671, 05:25:04; repeated by Grunander in the 2026-09-01 closing — "The optical accessory or the scope, that one is slightly different"). In State's Ex. 33 (ATF report on the Dremel and the safe-top cartridge cases) the two calculations read aloud — Dremel buttons (15.1) and the etched "test shot" .30-06 case (18.1) — are also "at least one trillion"; calcs 2–4 were expressly not read.
results.label: SUPPORTED

results.method: artifact_search.py find() (both readings) for 'reporting cap|cap|trillion|do not report|maximum' in day5 and for '[0-9][0-9.,]* (billion|million|trillion|quadrillion|quintillion)' across all transcripts; every numeric hit opened and read in context; Oliver's employer and title read from her own voir dire (day5 01:14:59).
results.divergence: Three precisions. (1) 'not a measured result' is loose: a probabilistic-genotyping calculation WAS run; ATF truncates the REPORT at 10^12, so each capped figure is a disclosed floor ('at least one trillion'), and Oliver said the true value 'could be a lot higher… quintillion, octillion.' (2) Oliver attributed the cap to comprehensibility, not to statistical limits: confronted with a NIST passage saying an LR reporting cap is chosen 'because of the limitation of biostatistical modeling and independence assumptions of STR loci,' she answered 'I believe we chose our cap for the reason I stated' and said she was unfamiliar with the referenced paper (01:38:55–01:39:36). Anyone using the cap to argue modelling limits is not resting on her testimony. (3) The 10^12 cap is the ATF's alone — the FBI report (State's Ex. 31, Bakker) carries 1.7 octillion and 30 quintillion, so ATF's cap explains nothing about those figures.
results.scope_limits: 'Only one non-capped figure' is verified for State's Exhibit 30's seven calculations (six capped, scope = 6.28 billion) and for every ATF likelihood ratio actually spoken on the record. It is NOT verified across all ATF calculations: three of Exhibit 33's statistical calculations were never read aloud, and neither ATF DNA report was read page-by-page. The finding is about reported LR magnitudes only; it says nothing about which propositions were compared, about contributor-number assumptions, or about how or when DNA was deposited (Oliver: none of the three reports can answer that).

results.isolated_answer: Amanda Bakker — forensic examiner, FBI Laboratory DNA Casework Unit, Quantico; author of State's Ex. 31, the FBI report on the towel and the screwdriver — was called by the DEFENCE (Burt) on Day 2 and sworn at 05:14:59. Under oath (day2.txt 05:25:15–05:30:29): FBI policy forbids an examiner stating or implying that a match provides "an absolute identification of the individual from whom the biological material originated" — "That is correct"; "You never said it was an absolute identification of Mr. Robinson, did you?" — "Correct. No, I did not" (L5543–5548); the DOJ Uniform Language policy provides that "[a]n examiner shall not assert that a likelihood ratio of any magnitude provides an absolute identification or source attribution of an individual to an evidentiary sample" — "That is correct. Yes, it does state that," and she followed it; then "You're not implying that those numbers, that a previous witness quoted and are stated in your report, provides an absolute identification of Mr. Robinson or Mr. Twiggs?" — "No, I'm not" (L5724–5728). She affirmed her reported conclusion was DOJ's "support for inclusion": evidentiary support for the inclusion of a known individual as a POSSIBLE CONTRIBUTOR. The "previous witness" is SBI Sgt. Jennifer Faumuina, who earlier the same day, over Burt's Rule 403 cumulative objection (overruled), read from Ex. 31: Item 7 = "Towel from around Mauser or rifle, Serial Number 8863" → "The DNA results from Item 7, sub 1 … are 1.7 octillion times more likely if Twiggs and T. Robinson are contributors than if Twiggs and an unknown, unrelated person are contributors" (05:10:57, L4877); Item 8 = "Screwdriver from perch" → "30 quintillion times more likely…" (05:11:41, L4913). Both readings precede Bakker being called at 05:14:18. A programmatic scan of all 456 of Bakker's transcript turns on Day 2 finds no occurrence of 'octillion', 'quintillion', 'trillion', 'billion', '1.7' or '30' as a magnitude — the only large number she volunteered was the general verbal scale (LR ≥ 1,000,000 = "very strong support for inclusion", 07:18:42).
results.label: SUPPORTED
results.method: artifact_search.py find() (both readings) for 'source attribution|absolute identification|the source of the DNA|octillion|quintillion' across all transcripts; then a Python pass that reconstructed every 'Ms. Bakker' speaker block in day2.txt and tested it for magnitude tokens. Speakers inferred from Q/A structure and content (the numeric recitations at 07:59 are in interrogative form and end 'correct?', so they are counsel's; Bakker's are the one- to two-word affirmations).
results.divergence: Three refinements, all of which narrow the claim. (1) Bakker's disclaimer is specifically of ABSOLUTE identification and SOURCE ATTRIBUTION — not of any bearing on source at all. In the same passage she affirmed her conclusion of 'support for inclusion' of a known individual as a possible contributor. Rendering it as 'the ratios do not identify either Robinson or Twiggs as a source' overstates her testimony unless 'absolute' is kept. (2) 'The examiner herself never uttered the figures' is literally true, but not the whole record: on cross, prosecutor McBride read both figures to her verbatim (07:59:30 and 07:59:58) and she adopted them — 'Correct. Yes.' and 'Yes.' She is therefore not a witness who avoided the numbers; she is one who never spoke them first. (3) Both ratios condition on Twiggs being a contributor in BOTH competing propositions (Twiggs + Robinson vs Twiggs + unknown unrelated), so neither figure tests Twiggs's presence at all — a point the 'naming Robinson' framing obscures.
results.scope_limits: Day 2 only, and only the FBI report (State's Ex. 31) on the towel (Item 7) and the screwdriver (Item 8). Says nothing about the ATF reports or Oliver's testimony, nothing about Bakker's Day 2 testimony on error rate, activity level, contributor number or stochastic effects beyond what is quoted, and nothing about the accuracy of the ratios themselves. The 'never uttered' finding is a null over the Rev transcript of Day 2 as banked — a machine transcript with unreliable speaker labels; it would not catch a figure garbled in transcription or mis-attributed to counsel.

results.isolated_answer: At the Utah County charging press conference of Sept 16, 2025 (banked Rev transcript), the ONLY confession question was put by a KUTV reporter at 35:58, immediately after an extended run of questions about the Robinson–Twiggs text messages: "For those that aren't of a legal mind, is this a confession, the text messages? Is that legally a confession? And is he cooperating since he's been taken into custody?" County Attorney Jeff Gray answered at 36:08 (L217–219): "Ultimately, a judge will determine that at trial." He then declined the cooperation half ("Again, I'm not going to comment on that"). The referent of the question — and so of the deferral — is the TEXT MESSAGES to the roommate, not Robinson's statements to his parents. On the parents' account, Gray said only (37:18) "What the family said is what I provided," after having read the mother's and father's statements out of the probable-cause narrative, and he repeatedly refused to comment further on the evidence or on whether the parents were still cooperating (38:33). Nothing in the presser records him characterizing, or declining to characterize, the statements Robinson allegedly made at his parents' home as a confession.
